newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Low Russian yields could spark industrial lending.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Low Russian yields could spark industrial lending.

text.p: Record low Treasury bill yields have raised the hopes of Russian businessmen and ministers that banks will now start lending to industry rather than raking in high returns in the government bond market.

But economists say the government must do more to reduce the budget deficit if yields are to fall further, while banks will not be willing to lend to the real economy until Russian industry is restructured.
In mid-May the T-bill market saw record low yields, which fell to 26.1 percent from more than 200 percent before last June's presidential election, and dealers forecast further falls.
Real interest rates fell to 10-20 percent in the first quarter of 1997, making investors rush into Russian equities, CentreInvest Securities brokerage said.
High-yielding GKO discount Treasury bills, which had previously soaked up most funds for investment, were becoming less attractive to banks, it said in a research note.
If nominal T-bill yields decline below 22 percent, Russia may fall in line with the growth trend of other Eastern European countries, it said.

"We expect GKO rates to decline even further in the second quarter of 1997, as the new government is fighting to hold the actual budget deficit down and is borrowing heavily through Eurobonds," CentreInvest Securities said.
"Thus, we could see investment rising, which will be the precursor of Russian GDP growth."
INVESTMENT VITAL TO REVIVE ECONOMY
Investment is vitally needed in Russia to re-ignite an economy which has been contracting since 1989, the last years of the Soviet Union.
The government, which had said economic growth will start this year, now forecasts 1997 GDP will be unchanged from 1996 while industrial output will be flat or rise by one percent.

Banks are increasingly willing to hold roubles rather than dollars, and the fall in T-bill yields is making them look for alternative instruments. The stockmarket, though near record highs, is too narrow and illiquid to absorb a huge amount of Russian investment.
Pavel Teplukhin, chief economist at Troika Dialog, said the core issue in attracting domestic investment is cutting the budget deficit.
"Instead of cajoling the market to push down the yields the Central Bank and the government should hire a thousand tax policemen and collect taxes," he said.

The government says it will not let the budget deficit widen, even though tax receipts are far below budgeted levels. It has said it is switching from borrowing on the domestic market to the international one, where funds are cheaper.
On the domestic market, it has been borrowing only enough to repay maturing issues for several months.

Teplukhin said that if the GKO yield fell to 20 percent annual in rouble terms Russia could see more lively investment which would take two forms -- acceptable credit rates and terms of a year or two instead of the current several months.
Currently, banks are reluctant to grant credits for over a year and the average rate is between 36 and 50 percent.

But other analysts said Russian industry still had to be restructured and a legal framework, including the possibility of using land as a security for loans, set up, for investment to flow into the real sector.

Andrei Yashchenko, a United City Bank analyst, said banks were unwilling to invest in industry, as management at many companies had failed to learn how to work under conditions of market economy and still did not understand how to use funds properly.
"The key question is how much management has adjusted to the new conditions and how effectively the funds will be used," he told Reuters.

Naderya Mukhetdinova, an economic analyst at the Federation Council upper house of parliament, said that in many cases companies did not have a proper development strategy and simply used credits to raise wages.
"If the real sector shows that it can at least start working properly, potential funds will flow in," she said.
Another reason for slow investment into the industry was low competitiveness of Russian goods, Mukhetdinova said.

But government decisions to restructure natural monopolies such as gas producer Gazprom and the national power company Unified Energy System, which should lead to lower energy prices, would help make Russian goods more competitive, she said.
But Yashchenko said the shortage of suitable companies to lend to could paradoxically cause banks to compete hard for the chance to lend to industry.
"There are too few reliable borrowers and this will inevitably lead to competition among banks for companies with a more or less stable financial situation," he said.
